# Conventions {.unnumbered}

This book uses a small set of visual conventions, which we
summarize here for the reader's reference.

## In code blocks

- Input lines carry no prefix.
- Output lines are prefixed with `#>`. The whole block therefore
  remains a valid R script, so that it runs without error when
  pasted into a console.
- Numbered discs in the code gutter (1, 2, 3) are annotations.
  The reader may hover over or tap them to read the
  annotation, or may read the numbered list below the block.

A minimal example:

```{.r}
library(dplyr)

penguins |>                                       # <1>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |>                  # <2>
  group_by(species) |>                            # <3>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g))
```
1. Start the pipeline with the `penguins` data frame.
2. Drop rows with missing body-mass values.
3. Compute the species-level mean body mass.

## In prose

- **Bold** marks a term on its first use.
- `monospace` marks code, file paths, and package names.
- `package::function()` disambiguates function ownership when
  the package is not obvious from context.

## Callouts

::: {.callout-note title='Note'}
Clarification that is useful but not essential on first read.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
A concrete check the reader should run. This is the book's
signature callout, and it appears after every non-trivial
example.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
A failure mode reported by past students of the course.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
An adversarial prompt for use with a language model, paired
with an explicit verification step.
:::

## Mathematical notation

We use conventional notation throughout. Vectors are bold
lower-case ($\mathbf{x}$); matrices are bold upper-case
($\mathbf{X}$); scalars and parameters are non-bold.
Estimators carry hats ($\hat\theta$). Sample size is $n$;
parameter dimension is $p$.
